title: Query Batching
statement:
Sending many one-key lookups as a single larger request is a common optimization. Write a class `QueryBatcher` that does it. Its constructor takes two arguments:

- `queryMultiple(keys)`, an async function. Given an array of string keys, it resolves with an array of the same length whose element `i` is the value for `keys[i]`. It never rejects.
- `t`, the smallest allowed gap in milliseconds between two calls of `queryMultiple`.

The class has one method, `getValue(key)`, which returns a promise that resolves with the string value for the string `key`. Every key must be sent to `queryMultiple` exactly once, and its promise resolves with the value that call returns for it. The rules for calling `queryMultiple`:

- If `getValue` is called and `queryMultiple` has not been called during the last `t` ms (or never), call it at once with just this key.
- Otherwise the key waits. As soon as `t` ms have passed since the previous call of `queryMultiple`, send **all** waiting keys together in one call, in the order they arrived.
- Two calls of `queryMultiple` are never less than `t` ms apart; the judge reports an error if they are.

All keys in a case are distinct. Each case gives `queryMultiple` as an object `{ delay, perKey }`: the function waits `delay + perKey * keys.length` ms (not at all when that is `0`) and then resolves with every key followed by `"!"`. Then come `t` and a list of `calls`, each `{ key, time }`: at `time` ms from the start, `getValue(key)` is called. The answer has one `{ resolved, time }` per call, the value its promise resolved with and the time it resolved, sorted by time, with ties in the order of `calls`. Cases never call `getValue` at the exact moment that `t` ms have passed since a call of `queryMultiple`, so you never have to decide which comes first.
constraints: queryMultiple is { delay, perKey } with 0 <= delay <= 1000 and 0 <= perKey <= 200
Each key is 1 to 10 lowercase letters, and all keys are distinct
No call of getValue happens exactly t ms after a call of queryMultiple
signature: List<Object> QueryBatcher(Object queryMultiple, int t, List<Object> calls)
api: class QueryBatcher { constructor(queryMultiple: (keys: string[]) => Promise<string[]>, t: number); getValue(key: string): Promise<string> }
notes:
## Intuition

The batcher alternates between two states. While it is **cooling**, a call of `queryMultiple` happened less than `t` ms ago, so new keys must wait. When the cooldown ends, everything that waited goes out in one call, and that call starts a new cooldown. If nothing waited, the batcher simply stops cooling, and the next key can go out at once. A single timer per call of `queryMultiple` is enough to drive this: when it fires, it either sends the waiting keys or switches the cooldown off. Each waiting key also needs its own promise, so the batcher stores the promise's `resolve` function next to the key and calls it once the batch's values arrive. (The brute force compares `Date.now()` with the time of the last call instead, and lets every waiting key await one shared promise for its batch.)

## Approach

1. Keep `waiting`, the list of `{ key, resolve }` not yet sent, and `cooling`, which is true while the last call is less than `t` ms old.
2. `getValue` creates a promise, puts its key and `resolve` in `waiting`, and calls `flush` at once when the batcher is not cooling.
3. `flush` with an empty `waiting` turns `cooling` off: the cooldown ended with nothing to send.
4. Otherwise it takes the whole list as `batch`, empties `waiting` and turns `cooling` on.
5. It calls `queryMultiple` with the batch's `keys` and, when the values arrive, resolves item `i` with `values[i]`.
6. It schedules the next `flush` for `t` ms later, the moment the cooldown ends.

## Example 1, step by step

`t = 100` and `queryMultiple` answers at once.

- 10 ms: `getValue("a")`; not cooling, so `flush` sends `["a"]`, which resolves with `"a!"` at 10 ms. The next `flush` is due at 110 ms.
- 20 ms and 30 ms: `"b"` and `"c"` arrive while cooling and wait.
- 110 ms: `flush` sends `["b", "c"]`; both resolve at 110 ms. The next `flush` at 210 ms finds nothing and turns `cooling` off.

The answer is `a!` at 10, `b!` and `c!` at 110.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) per `getValue` call, plus O(k) to split a batch of k keys' values.
- Space: O(n) for the waiting keys and their resolvers.

## Pitfalls

- Starting the cooldown when a batch **resolves** instead of when it is **sent**: in Example 3, `"e"` must go out at 250 ms although the batch sent at 110 ms is still running.
- Sending the first key after a quiet spell through the timer instead of at once delays it by up to `t` ms.
- Forgetting to turn `cooling` off when a cooldown ends empty leaves later keys waiting forever.
- Resolving by position needs the batch's own list: `waiting` may already hold new keys when the values come back.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `waiting` | keys not sent yet, each with the `resolve` of its promise |
| `cooling` | true while the last call of `queryMultiple` is less than `t` ms old |
| `batch` | the items sent together in one call |
| `keys` | the batch's keys, in arrival order |
| `values` | what `queryMultiple` resolved with; `values[i]` belongs to `batch[i]` |
